questions.q: A flywheel shooter works most like a...
wrong: Car's steering wheel
Bicycle's hand brake
Kitchen microwave oven
questions.explain: A flywheel is a heavy spinning wheel that flings game pieces, just like a baseball pitching machine spins a wheel to hurl a ball.

questions.q: What is inertia, for the flywheel?
questions.correct: The heavy wheel resisting changes to its speed
wrong: The wheel spinning faster all on its own
The battery slowly losing charge over time
The motor overheating during a long match
questions.explain: Inertia is a heavy wheel's resistance to speed change. It's slow to spin up, but once spinning it barely slows when a piece hits it — giving consistent shots.

questions.q: Why is a heavy flywheel preferred for competition?
questions.correct: Its shots stay consistent even during rapid fire
wrong: It spins up a great deal faster than a light one
It uses far less power from the robot's battery
It is much lighter to carry around the field
questions.explain: A heavy wheel barely slows when a piece hits it, so every shot leaves at nearly the same speed. A light wheel drops speed on each shot and misses.

questions.correct: Each shot slows it a lot, so shots are inconsistent
wrong: It is far too heavy to spin up quickly
It can never reach a high enough speed
It drains the robot's battery twice as fast
questions.explain: A light wheel spins up fast but loses a lot of speed on each shot, so the shots come out at different speeds and land in different places.

questions.q: Which motor type can report its own speed?
wrong: A plain DcMotor, with no encoder
A CRServo, using its setPower
A positional Servo, using an angle
questions.explain: Only DcMotorEx (the "extended" motor) can report speed with getVelocity(). A plain DcMotor can't, which is why the flywheel uses DcMotorEx.

questions.q: How many encoder ticks per revolution does this motor make?
wrong: 60 ticks per revolution
360 ticks per revolution
1 tick per revolution
questions.explain: The goBILDA 1:1 motor produces 28 ticks per output revolution. You use that number to turn encoder ticks into RPM.

questions.correct: Encoder speed in ticks per second
wrong: The motor's power from 0 to 1
The robot's heading in radians
The distance driven in inches
questions.explain: getVelocity() returns the encoder's speed in ticks per second. Divide by 28 (ticks/rev) and multiply by 60 to get RPM.

wrong: ticksPerSecond times 28, times 60
ticksPerSecond divided by 60, times 28
ticksPerSecond plus 28, times 60
questions.explain: RPM = (ticksPerSecond / 28) * 60. Ticks/sec → revs/sec (divide by ticks-per-rev) → revs/min (times 60).

questions.q: What does the toggle() command do?
questions.correct: Flips the flywheel on or off
wrong: Sets the flywheel to full power
Reads the flywheel's current RPM
Reverses the two drive motors
questions.explain: toggle() flips the spinning boolean, turning the flywheel on if it was off and off if it was on — called once per button press.

questions.q: Why check a deadzone before nudging the power?
questions.correct: To ignore tiny stick drift near the center
wrong: To make the flywheel spin much faster
To save battery while the wheel spins
To reverse the flywheel motor's spin
questions.explain: A stick rarely sits at exactly zero. The deadzone ignores tiny drift so the wheel's power isn't nudged constantly when you aren't touching the stick.

questions.correct: Trims the power up or down a little each loop
wrong: Sets the power to one single fixed value
Reads the encoder's total tick count
Prints the RPM onto the telemetry
questions.explain: nudge() creeps the stored power up or down by a small step (and clamps it), so the driver can fine-tune the shot strength with the stick.

questions.q: Why does a heavy wheel take a moment to spin up?
questions.correct: Its inertia resists the change to a higher speed
wrong: The motor is too weak to ever spin it up
The encoder slows the wheel down first
The battery must warm up before it spins
questions.explain: A heavy wheel's inertia resists speeding up, so setPower doesn't reach full RPM instantly — it ramps over about a second. Fire too early and the shot falls short.

questions.q: What two pieces of state does the flywheel remember?
questions.correct: Whether it's spinning and its power level
wrong: Its heading and its distance traveled
The battery voltage and the tick count
The intake speed and the hood angle
questions.explain: The flywheel remembers spinning (a boolean) and power (a double). update() applies power when spinning, or zero when off.

questions.correct: Real measured speed from the encoder
wrong: Commanded power from 0 to 1
Target angle for the hood
Distance to the hive in inches
questions.explain: getRpm() reads the encoder (getVelocity) and converts to RPM, so you see the wheel's REAL speed — no more guessing whether it's up to speed.

questions.q: Why use DcMotorEx instead of DcMotor for the flywheel?
questions.correct: Only DcMotorEx can measure the wheel's speed
wrong: DcMotorEx spins with about twice the power
A plain DcMotor cannot be reversed in code
DcMotorEx runs without needing any battery
questions.explain: You need to know the flywheel's real RPM, and only DcMotorEx offers getVelocity(). A plain DcMotor can set power but can't report speed.
